title: Mastering the Psychiatric HPI Interview Structure

slides.body: Master the psychiatric History of Present Illness (HPI) interview. Prevent clinical errors and build a precise differential diagnosis.
slides.headline: A Structured HPI Is Your First Defense Against Missed Diagnostic Clues

slides.body:
Chief Concern — The patient's primary symptoms, in their own words.
Timeline — Onset, duration, frequency, and course of symptoms.
Functional Impairment — How symptoms impact social, occupational, and daily functioning.
slides.headline: The 3 Anchors of the Psychiatric HPI

slides.body:
Location — Where is the symptom experienced?
Quality — What does it feel like?
Severity — How intense is it (e.g., 1-10 scale)?
Timing — Onset, duration, and frequency.
Context — What is happening when it occurs?
Modifying Factors — What makes it better or worse?
Associated Signs/Symptoms — What else occurs with it?
slides.headline: The 8 Dimensions of a Symptom

slides.body:
Mapping symptom timelines helps distinguish primary from secondary conditions.
A structured timeline reveals patterns that support or rule out specific diagnoses.
Start — Initial symptom onset.
Middle — Introduction of new symptoms or stressors.
End — Current presentation and functional status.
slides.headline: How Chronology Clarifies Diagnosis

slides.body:
✓ Current & past psychiatric medications, including adherence and side effects.
✓ Comprehensive safety assessment: SI/HI, self-harm, command hallucinations.
✓ Substance use history: type, frequency, last use, withdrawal symptoms.
✓ Relevant medical history to rule out organic causes (e.g., thyroid, neurological).
slides.headline: Essential HPI Safety & Systems Review

slides.body: "A templated HPI is a missed opportunity. Each patient's story is unique. Your documentation should reflect their specific narrative, not just a checklist of symptoms. This is where true clinical insight begins."
slides.headline: Field Note: Avoid the 'Copy-Paste' Trap

slides.body:
Chief Concern: "I have no energy and can't sleep."
Timeline: Worsening low mood and anxiety over 3 months after job loss.
Impairment: Difficulty concentrating at new job, avoiding social events.
Associated Sx: Reports constant worry, middle insomnia (waking at 3 a.m.), and decreased appetite.

For PMHNP students and nurses on their psych rotation, mastering the History of Present Illness (HPI) interview is fundamental. A poorly structured HPI can lead to missed diagnostic clues, inaccurate assessments, and an incomplete clinical picture. This framework is your key to building a strong differential diagnosis.

This carousel provides a step-by-step guide to conducting a thorough and effective psychiatric HPI. Swipe through to learn:

🔹 The Three Core Anchors: How to ground your interview in the patient's chief concern, timeline, and functional impairment.
🔹 The Eight Dimensions of a Symptom: A systematic approach to exploring every aspect of a patient's presenting problem.
🔹 Symptom Chronology: Learn how mapping the timeline of symptoms helps differentiate between complex psychiatric conditions.
🔹 Essential Checklists: A guide to crucial areas like medication history, safety assessment, substance use, and medical rule-outs.
🔹 Expert Field Notes: A reminder on the importance of personalized documentation over generic, templated notes.

Developing strong interview skills is crucial for both clinical practice and success on the NCLEX. This guide provides the structure you need to ask the right questions, every time.
